name: High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control
description: Master the High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control. Complete guide covering ceiling-elbow mechanics, carotid compression, and proven defensive counters.
summary: The High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control is a blood-choke finish that drives the choking elbow skyward to clamp both carotid arteries beneath the jawline, bypassing the chin-tuck defense that neutralizes the standard guillotine.
overview:
Few finishing situations in no-gi offer a more favorable risk-to-reward profile than this one: the choke threatens an immediate tap, while most failed attempts simply return the attacker to the same dominant Guillotine Control they started from. Starting from an established Guillotine Control position provides a significant mechanical advantage because the head is already trapped and posture is already broken, allowing the attacker to focus entirely on converting the grip configuration and finishing. The position eliminates the most difficult phase of any guillotine attack—securing the initial head control—and reduces the technique to a grip transition and squeeze.

The critical distinction from other guillotine entries is that the grip change happens from a position of existing control rather than during a scramble or shot defense. The attacker rotates the choking wrist so the blade of the forearm presses directly into the near-side carotid artery while the elbow climbs vertically, closing the far-side artery against the attacker's chest and shoulder. This dual compression produces a pure blood choke that can cause unconsciousness within seconds of full application, often before the defender recognizes the severity of the threat.

Strategically, the high elbow variation is the primary answer to the chin tuck defense that neutralizes standard guillotines. When the defender drops their chin to protect the trachea, the high elbow angle attacks behind and beneath the jaw, making chin position largely irrelevant. This forces defenders into secondary defense layers—posture recovery and hand fighting—which opens opportunities for the attacker to chain into sweeps or positional advancement when the choke itself is defended.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate if released promptly; potential for serious complications if held past unconsciousness

injury_risks.injury: Tracheal damage from excessive pressure or improper angle
injury_risks.recovery_time: 2-6 weeks for minor trauma; months for severe damage requiring medical intervention

injury_risks.injury: Cervical spine stress from defensive bridging or improper application
injury_risks.recovery_time: 1-3 weeks for minor strain; 3-6 months for significant injury

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum application time with constant awareness of partner's response
tap_signals: Verbal tap or any verbal sound of distress
Physical hand tap on opponent's body or mat
Physical foot tap on mat or opponent
Any loss of resistance or body going limp
release_protocol: Immediately release choking arm grip upon any tap signal
Lower choking elbow and remove shoulder pressure simultaneously
Release head control and create space by stepping back or opening guard
Monitor partner's breathing and consciousness for 10-15 seconds
Never reapply pressure once released, even if partner signals they are okay
training_restrictions: Never apply at competition speed during drilling or positional training
Never spike or jerk the submission—always apply smooth progressive pressure
Never continue pressure if partner's face changes color or shows signs of oxygen deprivation
Always maintain verbal communication during slow drilling phases
Never practice on partners with neck or throat injuries without explicit instructor approval
Always allow clear tap access—never trap both arms while finishing

variations_and_setups.description: Uses the palm-to-palm clasp with the choking hand gripping on top of the support hand, allowing a rotational squeeze that drives the wrist blade deeper into the carotid. Favored when the choking arm is already deep around the neck.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have deep arm penetration around the neck and can immediately close the palm-to-palm grip without repositioning

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Short choke high elbow from half guard top
variations_and_setups.description: When the opponent has half guard and you are in guillotine control from top, thread the choking arm shallow and use elbow elevation combined with hip sprawl pressure to compress the neck against your own chest. Requires less depth than the full wrap.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent's half guard prevents full guard closure and you cannot achieve deep arm penetration

variations_and_setups.description: From standing guillotine control, elevate the elbow to the ceiling position and sit back to closed guard, using the fall and hip extension to generate finishing pressure. The momentum of the sit-back amplifies the choke tightening.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have the guillotine secured standing and the opponent is defending the standard finish by keeping their hips low and base wide

attacker.name: High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control. Step-by-step ceiling-elbow finish, grip transitions, and counter responses.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control means you already own the most valuable real estate in guillotine finishing—deep head control with broken posture. Your task is converting the existing grip into the high elbow configuration and finishing before the defender can recover posture or strip your hands. The ceiling-elbow angle generates bilateral carotid compression that bypasses chin tuck defense entirely, making this the highest-percentage guillotine variation against technically proficient defenders. From Guillotine Control you have the luxury of working a deliberate grip transition rather than racing to secure the head during a scramble, which allows precise forearm placement across the arteries.
key_principles: Drive the choking elbow vertically toward the ceiling to close the far-side carotid against your chest and shoulder
Maintain zero space between your choking forearm and the opponent's neck throughout the grip transition
Use closed guard or high guard to anchor the opponent's posture down while you adjust the finishing angle
Rotate the wrist blade into the near-side carotid artery before elevating—depth first, then height
Keep your chin tucked and head pressure forward to prevent the opponent from creating extension to relieve the choke
Coordinate hip extension with elbow elevation to create opposing forces that amplify compression
setup_requirements: Established guillotine control with choking arm wrapped around opponent's neck at sufficient depth for the wrist blade to reach the near-side carotid artery
Opponent's posture broken forward with their head below their hips, limiting their ability to create space or posture up
Hands clasped together in a secure grip configuration with the support hand reinforcing the choking wrist or forearm
Guard engagement (closed guard, high guard, or butterfly hooks) preventing the opponent from stepping over or driving through to escape
Opponent's chin tuck or standard defense committed, creating the opening for the high elbow angle transition

execution_steps.description: Confirm your choking arm is threaded deep enough that the blade of your wrist crosses the front of the opponent's throat, sitting against the near-side carotid artery. If the grip is shallow across the chin or jaw, re-swim the arm deeper before proceeding.

Release your standard clasp and re-grip by cupping your choking hand over the back of your opposite hand or clasping at the wrist. Position your support arm so that pulling generates upward force on the choking elbow rather than horizontal squeeze.

Lock closed guard high on the opponent's back or establish tight butterfly hooks. Pull your knees toward your chest to break their posture downward and prevent any space creation during the grip transition phase.

Drive your choking elbow toward the ceiling by rotating your shoulder forward and up. This motion rolls the forearm blade into the near-side carotid while your chest and shoulder close over the far-side artery, creating bilateral compression.

Push your hips forward and slightly arch your back to create separation between your chest and the opponent's trapped head. This shearing force amplifies the choke by pulling the neck into the forearm blade while your body structure compresses from the opposite side.

With the elbow at maximum height, contract both arms and pull the opponent's head tightly into your chest while maintaining hip extension. The finish should produce rapid bilateral carotid occlusion—watch for tap signals within three to five seconds of full application.

If the opponent survives the initial squeeze, walk your hips slightly toward the choking side to increase the lever arm, or switch between marcelotine and standard high elbow grips. Small rotational adjustments of the forearm often find the artery when the initial angle is slightly off.

common_counters.counter: Posture recovery—opponent frames on hips and extends arms to lift head out of choking position
common_counters.your_response: Immediately pull guard tighter and use your legs to break posture back down. If they create significant space, switch to pulling the head down and re-establishing depth before re-attempting the elbow elevation.

common_counters.counter: Hand fighting—opponent peels at the choking wrist or forearm to strip the grip before the elbow reaches full height
common_counters.your_response: Keep elbows pinned tight to your ribs and forearm connected to your chest. If they get a grip on your wrist, rotate toward the choking side to increase pressure and make their grip less effective. Regrasp quickly if broken.

common_counters.counter: Von Flue counter—opponent allows the guillotine while passing guard and applies shoulder pressure to the neck
common_counters.your_response: Never hold the guillotine with open guard or while your opponent passes to side control. If they begin advancing past your guard, either finish immediately or release the grip and re-establish guard before they consolidate the Von Flue position.

common_counters.counter: Turning into the choke—opponent rotates their body toward the choking arm to create space between forearm and neck
common_counters.your_response: Follow their rotation with your hips and use the turn to transition to anaconda or darce choke setups. Their turn actually exposes them to head-and-arm choke variations that are higher percentage than fighting to maintain the original guillotine angle.

common_errors.error: Elevating the elbow before securing sufficient depth around the neck
common_errors.consequence: The forearm slides across the chin or jaw rather than compressing the carotid arteries, producing pain but no choking effect and burning grip endurance
common_errors.correction: Verify the wrist blade is across the front of the throat before initiating the elbow climb. If depth is insufficient, re-swim the arm deeper first.

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arms only while neglecting hip extension
common_errors.consequence: Rapid forearm fatigue without sufficient compression to produce a finish. The opponent can outlast the squeeze and escape when grip strength fails.
common_errors.correction: Coordinate hip extension with arm contraction to create opposing forces. The hips drive the neck into the forearm while the arms pull the head into the chest—both forces together finish the choke.

common_errors.error: Allowing space between the choking forearm and the chest during elbow elevation
common_errors.consequence: The far-side carotid remains open and the opponent can breathe through one side, turning a blood choke into an uncomfortable but survivable squeeze
common_errors.correction: Keep your shoulder rolled forward and chest pressed into the side of the opponent's neck throughout the elbow climb. The forearm and chest must work as a unified compression surface.

common_errors.error: Holding the guillotine with legs open or guard disengaged
common_errors.consequence: The opponent passes guard while you maintain the grip, setting up a Von Flue choke counter that reverses the submission entirely
common_errors.correction: Always maintain closed guard, high guard, or active butterfly hooks while finishing. If guard opens and you cannot re-close it, release the guillotine and re-establish guard position.

common_errors.error: Attempting the finish with the standard palm-to-palm grip instead of converting to the high elbow configuration
common_errors.consequence: The standard grip generates horizontal compression that the chin tuck effectively blocks, stalling the submission and wasting energy
common_errors.correction: Consciously transition to the high elbow grip by cupping or clasping at the wrist level, then drive the elbow vertically before squeezing.

common_errors.error: Pulling the opponent's head upward toward your face instead of into your chest
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for the opponent to turn and extract their head, while also reducing the mechanical advantage of the choke angle
common_errors.correction: Pull the head down and into your sternum while your elbow climbs. Think of curling the opponent's head into your chest rather than lifting it toward your chin.

training_progressions.focus: High elbow grip mechanics without resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner allows you to practice the grip transition from standard guillotine to high elbow configuration repeatedly. Focus on wrist blade placement, elbow elevation path, and clasp positioning. No finishing pressure—develop the motor pattern of the grip change. 20 repetitions per side.

training_progressions.focus: Coordinating hip extension with arm contraction
training_progressions.description: From established high elbow grip, practice the finishing squeeze with partner providing light resistance. Focus on hip drive timing, chest-to-neck connection, and monitoring partner's tap signals. Partner taps early to allow multiple repetitions safely. 10 controlled finishes per side.

training_progressions.focus: Converting from guillotine control to high elbow against active defense
training_progressions.description: Partner defends the grip transition using posture recovery and hand fighting at 50-70% intensity. Practice maintaining control during the transition, re-establishing depth when stripped, and timing the elbow elevation around defensive reactions. 3-minute positional rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Full application from guillotine control against progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Start in guillotine control with partner defending at full intensity. Attacker wins by submission or positional advancement using the choke threat. Partner wins by escaping guillotine control entirely. Reset after each resolution. Develops realistic timing and decision-making under pressure. 2-minute rounds, 5-8 rounds.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the High Elbow Guillotine specifically target and how does the elbow position affect compression?
flashcards.answer: The High Elbow Guillotine targets both carotid arteries simultaneously. The blade of the wrist or forearm compresses the near-side carotid directly, while the elevated elbow closes the far-side carotid by pressing it against the attacker's chest and shoulder. This bilateral compression produces a blood choke that causes unconsciousness within seconds when fully applied, as opposed to a tracheal crush that primarily causes pain.

trap: Cuts off air, not blood flow

flashcards.question: Why does the High Elbow Guillotine defeat the chin tuck defense that stops standard guillotines?
flashcards.answer: The standard guillotine attacks horizontally across the front of the throat, which the chin tuck blocks by interposing the jaw between the forearm and the trachea. The high elbow angle attacks from below and behind the chin—the forearm blade slides under the jawline to reach the carotid arteries regardless of chin position. The vertical elbow path makes the chin tuck irrelevant because the compression occurs beneath the jaw rather than through it.
flashcards.answer_line: Attacks under the jaw, not front

plausible: Works by cranking the neck harder

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts hand fighting your choking wrist during the grip transition—what adjustment prevents the strip?
flashcards.answer: Pin your elbows tight to your ribs and keep the choking forearm connected to your chest wall, eliminating the space needed for effective hand fighting. Rotate your body slightly toward the choking side to increase downward pressure on their grip hand. If they momentarily break your clasp, re-grip immediately at the wrist rather than trying to re-establish the full palm-to-palm configuration, then complete the elbow elevation before they can re-engage their hand fight.
flashcards.answer_line: Pin elbows to ribs, stay tight

trap: Release grip and reset from scratch

flashcards.question: What are the critical indicators that the choke is properly set and the opponent is approaching the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: Key indicators include the opponent's hand fighting becoming weaker or less coordinated, a visible color change in the face (reddening or darkening), the opponent's breathing becoming labored or producing gurgling sounds, and the cessation of active escape attempts replaced by static tension. The point of no escape occurs when the elbow reaches full ceiling height with zero gap between forearm and neck—at this point even releasing one hand from the grip maintains enough compression to produce unconsciousness.

plausible: Gasping loudly means it's not set
trap: Wait for opponent to go fully limp

flashcards.question: What is the proper release protocol when your training partner taps to the High Elbow Guillotine?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release the choking arm grip upon any tap signal—verbal, physical hand tap, foot tap, or body going limp. Lower the choking elbow and remove shoulder pressure simultaneously. Release head control and create space by opening guard and stepping back. Monitor your partner's breathing and consciousness for ten to fifteen seconds after release. Never reapply pressure once released, and be prepared to call for medical assistance if your partner shows signs of delayed response or confusion.

trap: Hold briefly to make the point

flashcards.question: How do you coordinate hip extension with arm contraction to generate maximum finishing pressure?
flashcards.answer: The hips and arms create opposing forces that amplify compression on the neck. Push your hips forward and slightly arch your back to drive the opponent's trapped neck into the forearm blade, while simultaneously contracting your arms to pull their head into your chest. The key timing is to initiate hip extension first to set the angle, then add the arm squeeze progressively. This coordination lets skeletal structure and body weight do the work rather than relying on grip strength alone.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins passing your guard while you hold the guillotine grip—what is the correct decision and why?
flashcards.answer: You must either finish the submission immediately before they consolidate the pass, or release the grip and address the guard pass with standard retention. Holding the guillotine grip while the opponent passes to side control exposes you to the Von Flue choke, where their shoulder pressure on your neck reverses the submission. The decision depends on how deep and tight your choke is—if the elbow is fully elevated and compression is bilateral, you can finish through the pass; if the grip is compromised, release immediately.
flashcards.answer_line: Finish now or release the grip

plausible: Hold on and let them pass

flashcards.question: In competition, what finishing adjustments maximize your success rate when the opponent is actively defending?
flashcards.answer: In competition, use rapid grip switching between standard and high elbow configurations to prevent the defender from settling into a single defensive pattern. Time the elbow elevation to coincide with the opponent's exhalation when their neck is momentarily thinner. Walk your hips toward the choking side to increase the lever arm. If the opponent stalls your finish, threaten positional advancement to mount or back control—their defensive reaction to the position threat often opens the neck for the choke finish.

plausible: Squeeze harder and wait it out
Stay in one grip, grind it out
trap: Give up choke, chase back control

defender.name: High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control Defender
defender.description: Defend against the High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control. Recognition cues, escape techniques, and survival strategies for BJJ practitioners.
defender.overview: Defending the High Elbow Guillotine from Guillotine Control requires recognizing the elbow elevation early and acting before the attacker completes the grip transition. The high elbow angle bypasses the standard chin tuck defense, so your primary survival tools are posture recovery, hand fighting the choking wrist, and creating angles that reduce compression on both carotid arteries simultaneously. Time is severely compressed in this position because the blood choke can produce unconsciousness within seconds once the elbow reaches full height, making early recognition and immediate decisive action essential. Your best outcomes come from preventing the grip transition entirely rather than trying to survive the fully locked choke.
key_principles: Recognize the elbow elevation early—once the elbow reaches ceiling position with full compression, escape becomes nearly impossible
Fight the choking wrist and forearm connection to the chest before the elbow climbs, not after
Posture recovery is your highest-priority defense: get your head above your hips to reduce the mechanical advantage of the choke angle
Create angles by turning into the choking arm to reduce bilateral carotid compression to single-side pressure
Never allow your opponent to maintain closed guard while finishing—fighting the guard open reduces their ability to control your posture
Tap early and decisively if the choke locks in—the blood choke window to unconsciousness is measured in seconds, not minutes
recognition_cues: Attacker's choking elbow begins rising vertically toward the ceiling rather than squeezing horizontally across your throat
Attacker releases standard palm-to-palm clasp and re-grips at the wrist level, indicating the high elbow grip transition
Increased pressure behind and beneath your jawline rather than across the front of your throat, indicating the forearm blade is targeting the carotid angle
Attacker's hips begin driving forward and extending while their guard tightens, indicating the coordinated finishing squeeze is beginning

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one hand fight on the choking wrist to prevent elbow elevation
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the attacker beginning the grip transition from standard to high elbow configuration, before the elbow reaches full height
defensive_options.if_successful: Strips or loosens the choking grip, allowing you to begin posture recovery and head extraction while the attacker re-establishes their clasp
defensive_options.risk: If you commit both hands to the wrist fight, you lose the ability to frame against the attacker's hips, potentially allowing them to advance position

defensive_options.action: Posture up explosively by framing on attacker's hips and extending your spine
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the choke is not yet fully locked and there is still space between the attacker's forearm and your neck to create movement
defensive_options.if_successful: Breaks the attacker's posture control and creates space to extract your head from the guillotine grip entirely, returning to a neutral position
defensive_options.risk: If the choke is already deep, posturing up can actually tighten the guillotine by driving your neck into the forearm blade

defensive_options.action: Turn into the choking arm and drive shoulder across to reduce bilateral compression
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the elbow is already elevated and posture recovery is not immediately possible, as a survival tactic to buy time
defensive_options.if_successful: Reduces dual carotid compression to single-side pressure, extending your survival window and potentially opening a path to extract the head
defensive_options.risk: Turning into the choke exposes you to anaconda and darce transitions if the attacker reads the rotation and re-threads their arm

defensive_options.action: Open attacker's guard and pass while defending the neck to threaten Von Flue counter
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker holds the guillotine from closed guard and you can create enough space to disengage their legs and advance to side control
defensive_options.if_successful: Passes the attacker's guard and applies shoulder pressure to their neck, reversing the submission threat with a Von Flue choke
defensive_options.risk: The attacker may finish the guillotine during the passing attempt if your neck defense lapses during the transition

escape_paths: Two-on-one grip strip on the choking wrist followed by explosive posture recovery and head extraction to neutral position
Turn into the choking arm combined with shoulder walk to reduce compression, then back step to clear the head
Open attacker's guard, drive shoulder into their neck, and pass to side control for Von Flue counter-pressure

favorable_outcomes.how: Strip the choking grip through persistent hand fighting on the wrist, then recover posture by framing on the hips and extending your spine. The attacker retains some head control but loses the submission threat.

Allow the attacker to maintain the guillotine grip while passing their guard to side control. Apply shoulder pressure to their neck for a Von Flue choke counter, forcing them to release the grip or be submitted themselves.

common_errors.error: Relying solely on chin tuck defense against the high elbow variation
common_errors.consequence: The high elbow angle attacks behind and beneath the jaw, making chin position irrelevant. You absorb full bilateral carotid compression while believing you are defended.
common_errors.correction: Combine chin tuck with active hand fighting on the choking wrist and immediate posture recovery. Chin tuck alone only works against standard guillotine angles, not the high elbow configuration.

common_errors.error: Attempting to posture up when the choke is already fully locked with the elbow at ceiling height
common_errors.consequence: Posturing drives your neck harder into the forearm blade, actually tightening the choke and accelerating the blood flow restriction
common_errors.correction: If the choke is fully locked, prioritize turning into the arm to reduce bilateral compression rather than posturing. Alternatively, tap immediately if escape is not available—the window to unconsciousness is very short.

common_errors.error: Fighting the choke with one hand while posting the other hand on the mat
common_errors.consequence: Single-hand defense lacks the strength to strip the grip against a fully committed two-arm choke. The posting hand provides no defensive value against neck compression.
common_errors.correction: Commit both hands to the choking wrist for maximum stripping power. Accept temporary positional disadvantage to survive the submission—you cannot be passed if you are unconscious.

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to tap when the choke is locked and escape attempts have failed
common_errors.consequence: Blood chokes produce unconsciousness within five to ten seconds of full bilateral compression. Delayed tapping risks involuntary loss of consciousness and potential injury.
common_errors.correction: Tap immediately and decisively when you feel bilateral carotid compression with no available escape path. There is no benefit to resisting a locked blood choke—the window to unconsciousness is too short to outlast.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the attacker is transitioning from a standard guillotine to the high elbow variation?
flashcards.answer: The primary cues are the attacker's elbow beginning to rise vertically toward the ceiling rather than squeezing horizontally, a grip change from standard palm-to-palm to a wrist-level clasp, and increased pressure shifting from the front of your throat to behind and beneath your jawline. You may also feel the attacker's hips begin extending forward as they coordinate the finishing mechanics.
flashcards.answer_line: Elbow rises, grip moves to wrist

trap: Ignore it, chin tuck still works

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap to the High Elbow Guillotine and when should you tap?
flashcards.answer: Tap clearly by slapping the attacker's body, your own body, or the mat with your hand, or by verbal signal. Tap immediately when you feel bilateral carotid compression with the elbow fully elevated and your escape attempts have failed. Do not attempt to tough out a locked blood choke—the window from full compression to unconsciousness is five to ten seconds. A clear early tap prevents injury and allows you to resume training safely.

plausible: Tap only if it really hurts
trap: Try toughing out a locked choke

flashcards.question: Why does chin tuck fail against the high elbow guillotine and what should you do instead?
flashcards.answer: Chin tuck defends against horizontal forearm pressure across the trachea by interposing the jaw. The high elbow angle attacks from below the jawline, sliding the forearm blade under the chin to reach the carotid arteries regardless of jaw position. Instead of relying on chin tuck alone, you must actively hand fight the choking wrist with both hands to prevent elbow elevation, and simultaneously work to recover posture by framing on the attacker's hips.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available when the attacker has fully locked the high elbow position?
flashcards.answer: Once the elbow reaches full ceiling height with bilateral carotid compression, your options are extremely limited. Your best chance is turning hard into the choking arm to reduce bilateral compression to single-side pressure, buying seconds to strip the wrist grip. If the attacker has closed guard locked, you can attempt to open the guard and pass to threaten a Von Flue counter. However, if neither escape is working within a few seconds, you must tap immediately to prevent loss of consciousness.
flashcards.answer_line: Turn into arm, strip the grip

trap: Keep fighting past a few seconds

flashcards.question: How does the Von Flue counter work and when is it a viable defensive option?
flashcards.answer: The Von Flue choke counter works by passing the attacker's guard while they maintain the guillotine grip, then applying heavy shoulder pressure into the side of their neck from side control. The attacker's own grip traps their arm in place, preventing escape from the counter-pressure. This is viable only when the attacker holds the guillotine with open guard or you can successfully open their closed guard during the defense. It is not viable if the attacker has tight closed guard and a deep choke—you must address the guard before attempting the pass.

trap: Try it against tight closed guard

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the grip transition and responding before the elbow reaches full height
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly transitions from standard guillotine to high elbow at 30% speed. Practice identifying the grip change, immediately committing both hands to the choking wrist, and beginning posture recovery. Focus on reaction time and correct hand placement. 15-20 repetitions per side.

training_progressions.focus: Executing full escape sequences against progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner applies the high elbow guillotine at 50-70% intensity. Practice the complete defensive sequence: wrist fight, posture recovery, head extraction. Include the turning escape and Von Flue counter as alternative paths. Partner resets grip if escape succeeds. 3-minute positional rounds with role switching.

training_progressions.focus: Realistic defense with full resistance and tap awareness
training_progressions.description: Start in guillotine control with partner applying full-intensity high elbow guillotine. Defender must escape or survive for the round duration. Emphasize tap discipline—tap early when escape is not available rather than risking unconsciousness. Develops honest assessment of defensive capabilities under pressure. 90-second rounds, 5-8 rounds.
